title: Witness History: Unforgettable Moments Captured Live Across the Globe
body:
The historic accord that birthed the World Trade Organization (WTO) was signed on 15 April 1994 in Marrakesh, Morocco, marking a watershed moment in the architecture of global commerce. The agreement, known as the Marrakesh Agreement establishing the WTO, transformed the multilateral trade framework that had been governed by the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) since 1947 into a full‑fledged institution with binding dispute‑resolution mechanisms, a permanent secretariat and a comprehensive set of rules covering goods, services, and intellectual property. The signing ceremony, attended by representatives of 123 nations, signaled a collective commitment to liberalise trade, reduce barriers, and create a predictable environment for international investment.

The creation of the WTO represented the culmination of two decades of pro‑trade negotiations that began in the aftermath of World War II. While GATT had successfully overseen successive rounds of tariff reductions, its provisional nature and limited scope left many emerging issues—such as services, agriculture, and the protection of patents—without a coherent global regime. The Marrakesh Agreement addressed these gaps by establishing the Agreement on Trade‑Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS), the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS), and the Agreement on Agriculture, among others. By embedding these sectors within a single institutional framework, the WTO offered a more integrated approach to trade policy, allowing members to negotiate across multiple domains and to enforce commitments through a structured, rules‑based dispute settlement system.

From a financial perspective, the WTO’s inception reshaped the calculus for investors, multinational corporations, and sovereign wealth funds. The certainty provided by a transparent, enforceable set of trade rules reduced the risk premium attached to cross‑border transactions, encouraging capital flows into emerging markets that had previously been wary of arbitrary trade restrictions. Moreover, the WTO’s emphasis on non‑discrimination—most notably the “most‑favoured‑nation” (MFN) principle—ensured that market access granted to one member could not be arbitrarily denied to another, fostering a more level playing field. This environment spurred a wave of foreign direct investment (FDI) in the late 1990s and early 2000s, particularly in sectors such as telecommunications, pharmaceuticals, and agribusiness, where the new rules on services and intellectual property opened previously closed markets.

Nevertheless, the WTO’s early years were not without controversy. Critics argued that the organization’s push for trade liberalisation disproportionately benefited wealthier economies, while imposing structural adjustment pressures on developing nations. The Agreement on Agriculture, for instance, required reductions in domestic subsidies and tariffs that many poorer countries feared would expose their farmers to volatile global prices. Likewise, the TRIPS agreement sparked fierce debate over access to essential medicines, especially in the context of the HIV/AIDS crisis in sub‑Saharan Africa. These tensions manifested in a series of high‑profile disputes and a growing coalition of nations seeking to reform the WTO’s agenda to better reflect development concerns.

In the decades since Marrakesh, the WTO has both expanded its membership—now encompassing 164 members representing over 98 percent of world trade—and faced new challenges. The rise of regional trade agreements, digital commerce, and geopolitical rivalries has tested the organization’s relevance. Recent disputes over steel and aluminium tariffs, as well as the contentious negotiations on e‑commerce rules, underscore the need for the WTO to adapt its rule‑making to a rapidly evolving economic landscape. At the same time, the institution’s dispute‑settlement mechanism remains a cornerstone of the global trading system, providing a peaceful avenue for resolving conflicts that might otherwise escalate into trade wars.

Looking ahead, the WTO stands at a crossroads. Its founding principles of openness, fairness, and predictability continue to underpin the global economy, yet the organization must reconcile the divergent interests of its diverse membership. Reform proposals—ranging from modernising the dispute‑settlement process to incorporating climate‑related trade measures—are already on the table. How the WTO navigates these reforms will determine whether it can sustain its role as the guardian of the rules‑based trading order that began in Marrakesh nearly three decades ago, or whether it will be eclipsed by a fragmented landscape of bilateral and regional accords. The decisions made in the coming years will shape not only the flow of goods and services, but the very architecture of global finance in the 21st century.
